45:16: The verse begins by listing great blessings bestowed on the Children of Israel. Notice that religious blessings come before worldly ones: the Scripture, judgment and prophethood, followed by good provision and distinction above the other peoples of their time. A community’s well-being is therefore measured first by the guidance, revelation and living example it has received, rather than by abundant food and wealth. Two interpretations are given for الْحُكْم [al-ḥukm, “judgment”]: rule and authority, or wisdom in understanding the Scripture. Through prophethood, revelation became a lived reality rather than merely a text preserved in memory. Allah also lavished good things upon them, freed them from bondage to Pharaoh and opened the way to many blessings, bringing together religious and worldly good. Yet mentioning religion first teaches that, without guidance, the remaining blessings cannot keep a community from losing its way.
45:17: The problem was not an unclear religious law. They had been given “clear directions in matters [of religion]”: clear commands and prohibitions. Nevertheless, disagreement arose after knowledge had reached them, not before. Its cause was “transgression against one another[5]”: rivalry over power, wealth and standing, until the knowledge that should have united them became a means of competition and alteration. This invites comparison with what happens when people become absorbed in minor issues and disputes among themselves, neglecting the great, clear teachings whose clarity they do not dispute. The history of the Children of Israel shows that turning away from a clear command can affect generations. They experienced wandering because they refused the command to enter the Holy Land, and a generation then grew up knowing the price of that refusal. Even if disputes are not fully settled in this world, the final judgment remains: “Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning their differences”.
45:18: After recounting the experience of a community that received clear proofs but then disagreed and turned away, the Prophet ﷺ is given this charge: “Then We put you [O Prophet] on a clear way of the religion; so follow it”. This new honor entails more than claiming to belong to a community; it carries the duty to follow, apply and spread the revelation. The Arabic word شَرِيعَة [sharīʿah, the divinely prescribed way] also evokes its linguistic origin: an accessible place from which water is drawn. Revelation is thus pictured as a clear path to life, sparing people the need to wander among competing desires in search of water. The contrast is decisive: divine guidance or human desires. An economic, social, political or personal outlook must therefore be assessed first by its agreement with what Allah has revealed, rather than by its popularity. Following revelation is not presented as a decorative addition. The verse guards against repeating the experience of those who abandoned clear teachings and then sought substitutes for them.
45:19: Pressure to abandon Allah’s law offers no real protection. Of those obeyed in defiance of Allah’s command, the verse says: “They cannot avail you at all against Allah”. Wrongdoers may support one another, but their mutual support cannot equal Allah’s protective care for those who are mindful of Him. This does not prevent benefiting from a non-Muslim’s worldly expertise, provided it does not conflict with a rule of the religious law. Benefiting from expertise is one thing; dependence that places human desires above revelation is another. The greatest loss is for a community to abandon Allah’s protection in pursuit of human protection that can do nothing for it when His judgment comes. The verse therefore teaches the heart that security, provision and victory ultimately come from Allah. Holding to His law is not withdrawal from the world; it preserves the standard that prevents blind imitation and acquiescence in wrongdoing.
45:20: The revelation available to people is more than religious information. It is “an insight for people”, through which a community sees its way, and “guidance and mercy”. The preceding account of the Children of Israel is therefore not meant to be read as a distant story, but as a mirror showing how a community comes to be replaced when it abandons divine law and follows desire. Although these insights are for people generally, guidance and mercy are specifically for “people who are certain in faith”. Knowing the text alone is not enough for it to guide a person’s conduct. Those who trust Allah’s promise and are certain of His judgment are the ones who dare to follow revelation when prevailing practices and surrounding pressures run against it.
45:21: The phrase “commit evil deeds” translates اجْتَرَحُوا السَّيِّئَات [ijtaraḥū al-sayyiʾāt, “committed evil deeds”]. Its wording evokes the image of a predator tearing at its prey, suggesting deep immersion in sin rather than a passing lapse. When divine law is removed from society and desire becomes the standard, people begin demanding a freedom detached from the effects of their actions on others. Yet society is like a ship: one group cannot bore a hole in its own part and claim that the harm concerns it alone. The Quran therefore rejects equating those who commit evil with those who believe and do good, in either life or death. Divine law and obedience are not inconsequential details, and breaking free from revelation cannot produce the same result. The words “How poorly they judge!” address anyone who imagines that the two paths lead to the same destiny.
45:22: The statement that Allah created the heavens and earth “for a true purpose” follows the rejection of equality between evildoers and believers. It connects the moral order with the order on which the universe itself rests: life was not created aimlessly, such that following divine law and abandoning it would amount to the same thing. Just as the heavens and earth stand upon truth and purpose, human life has a purpose and an accounting, and every soul will receive the recompense it has earned without injustice. To imagine that disobedience and obedience—or a society that chooses Allah’s revelation and one that abandons it for desire—could have an entirely equal outcome is therefore a judgment at odds with the truth upon which creation is founded.
